name: n1
responses: Negotiations should continue because maintaining communication can reduce miscalculation, clarify intentions, and preserve off-ramps during a crisis. Requiring coercion to stop before talks begin risks creating a self-reinforcing stalemate: each side can use continued pressure to block diplomacy. Talks do not have to mean conceding to coercion; they can proceed alongside deterrence, sanctions, or other measures while testing whether the adversary is willing to de-escalate.

Talks should proceed because maintaining communication can reduce miscalculation, clarify intentions, and create off-ramps before a crisis escalates. Refusing to engage until coercion ends can allow the adversary to control the timing of diplomacy and make escalation harder to reverse.

This does not mean rewarding coercion or conceding under pressure. Negotiations can continue alongside deterrence, defensive preparations, sanctions, and clear statements that coercive actions will not produce political gains. The key distinction is between **talking** and **giving in**: dialogue need not signal acceptance of the adversary’s behavior.
